intro_en: This is one of the most beautiful and enjoyable segments of the Israel National Trail - with flowing water, bathing spots and tall trees.
character_en:
(For those walking from the north) A continuous, gentle descent on a mostly comfortable trail, about 500 m of elevation in total. The climb from south to north is not hard, as it is mostly gentle.
In the central section, between Ein Yakim and the Sechvi Pools, there are several shallow pools of clear water that are pleasant for bathing. After a rainy winter the stream may flow for several kilometres further south.
The trail alternates between shade and full sun. The last 5 km, from Ein Seter to the road, are mostly exposed. In hot weather it is best to walk them towards sunset.
shortcuts_en: There are exit points towards Safed via Nahal Sechvi or Sheikh Kuweis.
transport_en:
Moshav Meron. Kibbutz Kadarim, about 2 km from the end point.
Recommended lodging: camping at the Mount Meron Field School.
pois_en: Flowing water, bathing pools and old fruit-tree orchards between Ein Yakim and the Sechvi Pools. Beautiful blooms in late winter and spring in the open sections - Nahal Meron and the stretch south of Ein Seter. Old flour mills, Nahal Meron, Ein Yakim, Sechvi Pools.
important_en: The Nahal Amud Nature Reserve, between Ein Yakim and the Sechvi Pools, is a reserve with an entrance fee. The payment point is not on the Israel National Trail but up above, yet the ranger is entitled to request payment from hikers in this section. In practice, however, trail hikers are usually not asked to pay.

The entire segment passes through a declared nature reserve with no overnight campsite, so sleeping along the stream is forbidden. Anyone who cannot complete the whole segment in one day must exit via Nahal Sechvi or Sheikh Kuweis.

In summer it is recommended to walk a shortened route, in the sections where there is water, to avoid walking in the hot hours - and to carry plenty of drinking water. Hiking the dry part of Nahal Amud, from Sheikh Kuweis to Road 85, is not recommended.
description_en:
From the Meron campsite (the hairpin bend) we head east through an underpass beneath the Parod-Meron road and reach Lower Nahal Meron, a tributary of Nahal Amud. The walking is mostly easy, and partly shaded. There may be a light flow in winter and spring. The Israel National Trail is accompanied here by black trail markings as well.
After about an hour's walk we reach a junction with a red-marked trail - a stepped trail that climbs south to the "A-Tina Police Station" and to the Israel Nature and Parks Authority car park.
From the junction with the red trail, the Israel National Trail descends to the left to Ein Yakim (in Arabic, Ein a-Tina - the Fig Spring). Ein Yakim is the spring with the largest discharge among the springs of Nahal Amud. Today the water emerging from the spring flows into the stream, to the delight of nature and hikers. In the past, the spring served as the water source for the city of Safed; its water was pumped and piped up to the city. To protect this important water source, the British built the police building above the spring after the disturbances of 1938.
The spring's name, Yakim, comes from one of the 24 priestly divisions that served in the Temple (each division served two weeks a year). The Yakim division was based in the Safed area, and its other name, Pashhur, gave its name to the plateau south of Safed - Ramat Pashhur.
A short walk from Ein Yakim we reach a trail junction - the Israel National Trail and the black trail turn left into the streambed. The blue trail continues straight along the southern bank, through terraces and orchards, to the Sechvi Pools.
The Israel National Trail crosses the stream on an aqueduct bridge and continues parallel to the flowing channel on a ledge above it, among tall trees and lush vegetation, in almost complete shade. The tall tree with palm-shaped leaves and round fruits, which sheds its leaves in winter, is the Oriental plane - a tree that grows mainly in the north of the country along the banks of flowing streams. In the Middle Ages the Arabs called the stream Wadi Dilbiya, after the Arabic name of this impressive tree.
In the past the stream was also called Wadi a-Tawahin - the Valley of the Mills, after the flour mills built along it. Along Nahal Meron and Nahal Amud there are about 20 historic flour mills, several of which have been restored by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority.
The water-powered mills operated until the early 20th century. The stream's water was channelled by aqueducts to the top of the chimney-like shafts above the mills. The water falling down the shaft turned the paddle wheel (the "turbine") set at the bottom of the mill building, beneath the lower opening of the shaft. The upper millstone (the "runner") was connected to the paddle wheel by an axle and turned on top of the lower stone (the "bedstone"). Wheat grains were poured between the stones from a wooden hopper hung above them, and the ground flour was collected around the bedstone.
At the confluence of Nahal Meron and Nahal Amud, we cross the channel of Nahal Amud and turn south, following the direction of flow. After a few minutes' walk we reach the Sechvi Pools: tall plane trees shade natural pools that are clear, beautiful and enjoyable for all ages. Beside the pools are the remains of a flour mill. This is a recommended spot for a break and a rest. Bathers take note: bathe according to the reserve's guidelines and with care, as the rocks beside the pools are sometimes slippery.
At this point it is possible to shorten the route, leave the Sechvi Pools and climb north up Nahal Sechvi on a green-marked trail towards Safed.
Nearby is the Mabtasha - a name meaning a wool-processing mill (fulling mill), which operated much like the flour mills, by water power. The mill was once given the name "Batan" - meaning wool processing in Spanish. The name dates from the 16th century, when Jews who had arrived after the expulsion from Spain settled in Safed, bringing the wool industry with them. Several flour mills in Nahal Amud were then converted into fulling mills - and water power drove wooden hammers that beat the sheets of wool.
From the Sechvi Pools, the Israel National Trail continues down Nahal Amud, together with the black markings, heading south. The water in the streambed dwindles until it disappears into the ground, and the "wet" section of Nahal Amud comes to an end. The vegetation opens up at times and the walking becomes more exposed to the sun.
This part of Nahal Amud was once called Wadi Limon: "and in the valley west of Safed, down the mountain where the water mills stand on the Dulbai river, there grow citrons" (Hibat Yerushalayim, mid-19th century).
Before the next trail junction, about 2.5 km from the Sechvi Pools, we pass several more well-preserved flour mills. At the junction a blue trail heads east, climbing steeply to Sheikh Kuweis and Ein Kuweis - and from there to the Safed industrial zone. This is another exit point for those who want to shorten the walk - and it is highly recommended to do so in summer and on hot days.
The Israel National Trail continues with the black markings down the stream. After a stretch, the trail climbs onto the right bank to bypass a high waterfall. The side of the trail facing the steep channel is protected by a safety railing. At the end of the bypass we pass the confluence of Nahal Seter with Nahal Amud, where a blue trail climbs to the right towards Har Mitzpe HaYamim. The Israel National Trail continues to the left, descending back into the streambed with the help of an iron ladder.
After crossing the channel, the trail climbs the opposite bank. Before the climb, you can try to locate Ein Seter, a small hidden spring (as its name suggests) about 150 m downstream from the crossing point. In some years, dripping water can be found here at the mouth of a niche on the left (eastern) wall of the channel. From the spring we return to the Israel National Trail. Note: do not drink the water, due to the risk of contamination!
We climb and walk along the eastern bank. The trail bypasses a waterfall and a canyon-like stretch of the stream. Along the bypass it is advisable to slow down, pay attention and take care, because the channel wall to the right of the trail is steep. At the end of the bypass, the trail descends back to the streambed.
In the channel we see plane trees and oleander bushes - two plants that grow in watery environments (moist habitats). Here, in the dry channel, they obtain the water they need through deep roots that reach water deep beneath the streambed. The oleander blooms in summer with pink flowers. When its branches or leaves are wounded, they secrete a highly toxic white sap.
After a short walk, the trail leaves the channel onto a dirt road. We are at about 100 m above sea level; the climate here is hot, and accordingly the Mediterranean vegetation typical of the Galilee gives way to steppe vegetation. The prominent tree here is the Christ's thorn jujube, of tropical Sudanese origin.
After a short walk along the dirt road, we see ahead the high bridge of Road 85 built over Nahal Amud. The Israel National Trail continues straight along the channel to beneath the bridge. To reach the end point at the car park beside Road 85, we continue along the road that climbs to the left.
nearby_en: A beautiful view of the Sea of Galilee from the village of Kahal.
